problem: Existing navigation/VLN work targets 360-degree image datasets and 3D simulators (R2R-style), and cannot be directly applied to immersive VR applications; VR navigation support is limited to pre-scripted guides or app-specific built-in AI.
motivation: VR is growing fast and many new, diverse environments will appear, so automated testing/exploration needs a navigation solution that generalizes across VR apps without per-app training. Navigation is a fundamental first step for automated VR exploration testing, and LLMs' broad knowledge could interpret unseen VR scenes from screenshots.
key_idea: A training-free LLM pipeline that turns VR screenshots into text plus grid-coordinate scene context, classifies the user's navigation request into a refined taxonomy, uses a multi-LLM vote to judge goal completion, and maps decisions to low-level controls via function calling.
insight: Frozen LLMs can reliably execute basic actions (21/21) and direct visible-goal navigation (16/18) across unseen VR scenes, but the cost is latency: the Comprehensive Interpreter takes about 72% of per-turn time (~49 s/turn) and the 3-LLM voter about 17%. Exploratory scanning shows LLMs struggle to decide when to stop (2 to 12 rotations for the same 360° scan), suggesting weak reasoning over image sequences and a need for context management. No ablations are reported, so the contribution of individual components is not isolated.
method: Comprehensive Interpreter: GPT-4o processes each VR screenshot in two ways: a chain-of-thought textual description of objects and features, and a visual interpretation obtained by overlaying a grid on the screenshot and asking for object coordinates; both are merged into scene context.

Pre-defined Navigation Categories: refined taxonomy (from Wu et al.'s VLN survey) with Semantic Interpreter (non-movement queries), Action Navigator (Movement/Stability executors), and Goal Navigator (Direct vs Exploratory goal).

Decision Voter: classifies the query into a category; for goal navigation, three LLMs (GPT-4o, Grok-2, Gemini-2.5-Flash) majority-vote whether the goal is reached (GOAL_REACHED stops navigation, otherwise GOAL_PROGRESS).

Decision-to-Control Mapping: OpenAI function calling exposes basic actions (move_forward/left/right(duration), rotate left/right, look_up/down, scan_360) as JSON functions, and the model chooses the function and parameters.
Closed-loop execution: capture screenshot, interpret, vote, act, repeat over multiple turns in a Unity simulator without a headset.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen) for interpreter and control mapping; GPT-4o + Grok-2 + Gemini-2.5-Flash (frozen) as voters
setting.observation: monocular stereoscopic VR screenshots of the user's FOV (RGB), with grid overlay
setting.action_space: discrete high-level control functions with duration parameters (move forward/left/right, rotate left/right, look up/down, scan_360), each ~2 s
setting.simulator: Unity (three Unity VR assets: Highway, Ship, Country House), no physical headset

numbers.extra: 6 attempts x 3 Unity VR environments, one task per environment; no standard benchmark
numbers.evidence: Tables 3-5 (Direct Goal-oriented navigation) and text: "16 out of 18 attempts were ultimately successful"; abstract: 89% success rate

numbers.extra: each action designed to last 2 s
numbers.evidence: Table 2: Overall Average overhead 0.74; text: all 21 basic commands executed successfully

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark used; custom small-scale Unity VR evaluation (18 goal attempts, 21 action queries, 9 scan attempts). Success rates are given per-environment only in tables (Highway 6/6, Country House 5/6, Ship 5/6). Exploratory scanning was measured only by rotations and time (avg 41.1 s per scan), with no success rate.
results: NavAI executed all 21 basic action commands (avg overhead 0.74 s) and achieved an 89% success rate (16/18) on direct goal navigation across three Unity VR environments. Efficiency is poor: ~49.4 s per turn and ~8 turns per attempt (up to ~395 s). Exploratory scanning is inconsistent (2-12 rotations). No baselines are compared.
limitations: High latency (~49 s/turn) from remote LLM calls for interpretation and sequential multi-LLM voting makes it unsuitable for real-time use.
LLMs cannot consistently decide stopping conditions in exploratory scanning tasks (2-12 rotations), reflecting weak multi-image context handling.
Very small evaluation: one task per environment, 6 attempts, three scenes, no baselines or ablations, and Semantic Interpreter tasks not evaluated.
